title: Will Marion Cook, Abbie Mitchell and the broken violin
summary: Whaley explains who Will Marion Cook was, why he broke his violin in Chicago when denied first chair, and Hinton recalls him conducting in 1933.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Oh, yeah. Marion Cook, when he was in Chicago playing with the symphony band, he broke his violin and declared he wouldn't play no more, see. And when they wanted piano player, he said, I can go to Boston and get all the piano players I want, good piano players, all them piano players were good.
Since you just brought up Will Marion Cook, for the record, tell the people who Will Marion Cook was.
Will Marion Cook was one of the greatest violinists in the world. He was rated third amongst the great musicians.
He was a black violinist.
Yeah.
Baltimore, was he?
From Baltimore. No, he was from -- I guess -- no, he was from North Carolina, -- what's that place there?
Well, --
But, anyway --
But he was a great violinist. Where did he study?
He went to Europe. He studied over in Europe and came back and became a very great musician.
And he was a composer also, wasn't he?
Yeah, I think he was.
He wrote some things like Melinda Lou? Remember that, Melina Lou? His wife -- what was his wife's name? She was a great singer, Abb--
Abbie Mitchell.
Abbie Mitchell.
She sang that -- 'Won't you come with me in my great teepee and let me fold you in my' -- something like that.
She also sang a song of (inaudible) called, 'Linda Lou, honey, did you hear that mockingbird sing?'
Oh, yeah.
Honey, he was singing so sweet in the moonlight.
She sang --
Do you remember that?
No, I don't remember that. She sang in the show that Eubie Blake and Noble Sissle had.
What was the name of the show?
Won't you come with me in my big teepee? Oh, what was the name of that show?
Shuffle Along?
Suffle Along.
Shuffle Along.
Yeah.
And she was a singer in that show, huh?
Beg your pardon?
She was a singer in that show.
Oh, yeah. I remember that show.
And you mentioned him breaking up his violin. Why did he break up his violin? In Chicago, did you say it was?
In Chicago, yeah.
Why?
See, he was supposed to be first violinist.
I see.
And I don't know, some -- they wouldn't put him because he was a black man. They wouldn't put him first so he broke his violin up and said he wouldn't play no violin anymore.
I don't think he ever did, either.
No. He was a great guy.
He was also a friend of Eubie Blake. Eubie knew him very well.
Oh, yeah.

I remember my first recollection as a young man, of playing in a big orchestra. It was in 1933, in Chicago World Fair. And they had all of the -- they had a black evening there, a black achievement evening. And Eubie Blake and Will Marion Cook were two of the guest conductors. And it was my first chance to play in a big orchestra, under the baton of Eubie Blake.
